newsitem.title: FRANCE: Vandal seeks forgiveness for Jewish grave outrage.
newsitem.headline: Vandal seeks forgiveness for Jewish grave outrage.

text.p: One of four French neo-Nazis on trial for the 1990 desecration of a Jewish cemetery in southern France tried to apologise on Tuesday to the widow of a man whose body was unearthed during an anti-Semitic rampage.
Yannick Garnier, 27, a former skinhead, approached Madeleine Germon and said his acts of "madness" had been driven by anti-Semitism.
"At the time I was an anti-Semite," Garnier told the widow quietly, adding that he had wanted to write to her to ask her forgiveness.

The attack on the centuries-old graveyard, in which the recently-buried body of Felix Germon was disinterred and his sodomisation simulated with a beach umbrella, provoked disgust throughout France and the world.
"But we are all Jews at the start," cried Germon "God is Jewish, Adam and Eve were Jewish, we are all human beings.
"They are monsters, vermin. I can't forgive them," she said before turning to the four men. "Why did you do it?" she asked.
Garnier's sudden confession last July lead to the arrest of his alleged accomplices and capped a six-year investigation that had been turning in circles.
Garnier, Olivier Fimbry, 31, Bertrand Nouveau, 28, and Patrick Laonegro, also 28 and described as the ideolologist of the group, face up to two years in prison if convicted.
A fifth member of the group, Jean-Claude Gos, had since died in a motorcycle accident.
Earlier in the day, the defendents described the night of May 8, 1990 -- which they had chosen because it was the anniversary of Germany's World War Two surrender -- in almost graphic detail.
"We lifted the coffin with a watering hose," said Nouveau. "Then we broke the cover. Gos decided to take out the corpse and lay it on a tomb. The odor and the sight horrified us."
At that point in the testimony, Madeleine Germon left the courtroom, supported by her lawyers.
The descration, in which 34 graves were wrecked, sent hundreds of thousands of people to the streets in a protest march led by late president Francois Mitterrand.

It also drew widespread condemnation of extreme-right National Front party leader Jean-Marie Le Pen, who was blamed for having encouraged such acts with his anti-Semitic rhetoric and calls to expel France's three million immigrants.
Le Pen protested his innocenece, complaining he was the victim of a witchhunt.

At the time of their arrests, investigators said all four were either members or sympathisers of the tiny Nationalist French and European Party (PNFE) which became known in the late 1980s in connection with a series of attacks on Arab immigrants
Joseph Sitruk, the Grand Rabbi of France, in court to testify said that "all of France was insulted, humanity was diminished."
"They didn't kill anyone, but they killed everyone. I'm not asking for any punishment, but that a lesson be learned," he said.
